fields.definition: A recording of an electric guitar or bass captured straight from the instrument through a direct box (DI), taken before any amplifier or speaker, so the track holds the raw, unamplified instrument signal.
fields.plain_english: It is the clean guitar sound recorded straight from the guitar, with no amp added. You can send it through an amp later to shape the tone.
fields.purpose_function: It captures a clean, uncolored version of the performance so tone decisions such as amp and effects can be made or changed later, and it provides a pristine signal for re-amping.
fields.practical_application: Engineers split the guitar signal and record the DI to its own track alongside the miked amp, so they can re-amp or blend it during mixing.
common_mistakes: Recording only the DI and no amp, then having no usable tone if you cannot re-amp later
Plugging a high-impedance guitar into a low-impedance line input, which weakens and dulls the signal
Assuming the raw DI sound is a finished guitar tone rather than a starting point
scenario_contexts: Tracking a guitar part with both a miked amp and a DI so the producer can revisit the tone in the mix
Recording a bass DI for a clean, tight low end that sits well with the drums
Capturing a scratch guitar quietly at home for later re-amping in a studio

sources: Radial Engineering technical documentation (DI and Reamp)

fields.definition: A bass guitar whose fingerboard has no metal frets, so the player's finger stops the string directly against the smooth board; this allows continuous pitch, slides, and vibrato but requires precise finger placement for accurate intonation.
fields.plain_english: It is a bass with a smooth neck and no metal frets. The player must place each finger in exactly the right spot to play in tune. Notes can slide smoothly, a bit like a singing voice.
fields.purpose_function: It gives a smooth, singing tone with expressive slides and vibrato (the characteristic 'mwah' sound) that a fretted bass cannot produce, at the cost of harder intonation.
fields.practical_application: An engineer records a fretless bass much like any bass but watches tuning closely, often using a clean DI and gentle compression to capture the finger-slide and 'mwah' character.
common_mistakes: Expecting perfect intonation without careful finger placement, since there are no frets to fix the pitch
Confusing a fretless bass with a lined fretless; the lines only mark positions and are not frets
Choosing bright, clanky processing that hides the smooth, vocal tone the instrument is known for
scenario_contexts: Recording a jazz or fusion bassline that needs smooth slides between notes
Tracking a ballad where the singing, expressive fretless tone supports the vocal
Editing a fretless take where slight tuning drift must be checked before comping

sources: Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments

No acceptable source (AES, a recognised professional text, or manufacturer technical documentation) defines it. The only real referent is the drum 'Moongel' damper pad, documented solely on vendor and marketing pages, which do not qualify and belong to a different topic (percussion damping). The term appears coined or misfiled for this packet and needs human review to confirm the intended sense.

fields.definition: Sound captured by a microphone from directions away from its central front axis (the on-axis line it points along); because most microphones are less sensitive and less bright off-axis, off-axis pickup sounds darker and quieter than on-axis pickup.
fields.plain_english: It is the sound a mic picks up from the side or at an angle instead of straight ahead. That angled sound is usually quieter and less bright than sound hitting the mic head-on.
fields.purpose_function: Understanding off-axis pickup lets an engineer shape tone and control bleed by aiming a mic toward or away from a source, since the off-axis level and frequency response differ from on-axis.
fields.practical_application: On a guitar cab, an engineer angles the mic off-axis to the speaker cone to tame harsh highs, and points mics away from other instruments to reduce their off-axis bleed.
common_mistakes: Assuming a mic hears all directions equally, when off-axis sound is quieter and often duller
Ignoring that off-axis pickup colors tone unevenly, so different frequencies drop by different amounts
Blaming the amp for a dull recording when the mic was simply aimed too far off-axis
scenario_contexts: Angling a dynamic mic off the center of a guitar speaker to soften harsh highs
Positioning a vocal mic so a nearby amp lands off-axis and bleeds in less
Choosing the mic angle on a cab to balance brightness against a boomy on-axis tone

fields.definition: A bass guitar that uses passive pickups and passive tone and volume controls with no onboard powered preamp or battery; its high-impedance output relies entirely on the magnetic pickups and simple passive circuitry.
fields.plain_english: It is a bass with no battery and no powered circuit inside it. The pickups make the sound on their own. The signal is weaker, so it needs a good input to sound full.
fields.purpose_function: It delivers a natural, traditional bass tone and simple, reliable operation, but its weak high-impedance signal needs a proper high-impedance input to avoid tone loss.
fields.practical_application: When recording a passive bass, the engineer uses an instrument-level, high-impedance DI input so the pickups are not loaded down, keeping the low end and clarity intact.
common_mistakes: Plugging a passive bass into a low-impedance line input, which loads the pickups and dulls the tone
Expecting the loud, hot output of an active bass and setting the preamp gain too low
Thinking passive means lower quality, when many classic bass tones come from passive instruments
scenario_contexts: Recording a vintage-style passive bass through a high-impedance DI for a classic tone
Setting preamp gain higher to match the lower output of a passive bass
Troubleshooting a thin, dull bass DI caused by an input impedance that is too low

sources: Radial Engineering technical documentation (DI and instrument impedance)

fields.definition: A device that converts a recorded line-level, low-impedance signal (from an interface or console output) back into an instrument-level, high-impedance signal, so a dry DI recording can be sent out to guitar pedals and amplifiers; it is essentially a reverse DI box, typically using a transformer, a level control, and a ground-lift switch.
fields.plain_english: It is a small box that turns a recorded guitar track back into a normal guitar-level signal. That lets you feed the recording into a real amp or pedals. It works as if the guitar were plugged in live.
fields.purpose_function: It matches the studio's line-level output to the instrument-level input an amp expects, avoiding the harsh, weak, or noisy result of plugging a line output straight into an amp.
fields.practical_application: The engineer patches the interface output through the re-amp box, then into a pedalboard and amp, adjusting the box's level so the amp sees a normal guitar signal.
common_mistakes: Plugging a line output straight into an amp instead of using a re-amp box, which causes an impedance mismatch and poor tone
Confusing a re-amp box with a DI box, since they convert signals in opposite directions
Ignoring hum from a ground loop between the interface and amp instead of using the box's ground-lift switch
scenario_contexts: Sending a recorded DI guitar out to several amps to audition tones after tracking
Using the box's ground-lift to kill hum when connecting the studio to a guitar amp
Reshaping a bass DI through a real amp and cabinet during mixdown

sources: Radial Engineering Reamp Station user guide (manufacturer technical documentation)

fields.definition: The process of playing a previously recorded dry signal (usually a DI guitar or bass) back out through a re-amp box into an amplifier, pedals, or effects, then miking and recording the result to a new track; it lets amp and tone choices be made or redone after the performance is captured.
fields.plain_english: It means running a clean guitar recording through a real amp later, then recording that amp sound. You can change or perfect the tone after the player has gone home.
fields.purpose_function: It separates the performance from the tone, so engineers can try different amps, mics, and settings without asking the musician to replay the part.
fields.practical_application: After tracking a DI, the engineer re-amps it through chosen amps and mic positions during mixing, dialing in the exact tone the song needs.
common_mistakes: Trying to re-amp from a line output without a re-amp box, causing an impedance mismatch and a weak, harsh tone
Not recording a clean DI in the first place, leaving nothing to re-amp later
UNSAFE: Running a loud amp at high volume during long re-amping sessions without hearing protection; sustained high sound levels risk permanent hearing damage.
scenario_contexts: Re-amping a scratch DI guitar through a boutique amp to upgrade the final tone
A producer re-amping bass through multiple cabs to blend a clean and a distorted tone
Fixing a good performance recorded with a bad amp sound by re-amping it later

fields.definition: Techniques and enclosures used to acoustically isolate a guitar or bass speaker cabinet so it can be miked at high volume without excessive bleed into the room or other microphones; methods range from isolation cabinets (iso boxes) to separate rooms, baffles, and acoustic enclosures.
fields.plain_english: It is any way to box off or separate a speaker cabinet. That keeps its loud sound from leaking into other mics or the room. You can crank the amp and still get a clean recording.
fields.purpose_function: It lets an engineer capture a driven amp tone at realistic volume while controlling bleed, room sound, and noise for the players and neighbors.
fields.practical_application: The engineer places the cab in an iso box or separate room, mics it inside, and monitors from the control room, keeping stage volume low during tracking.
common_mistakes: Cramming a cab into a small sealed box without treatment, creating boxy resonances that ruin the tone
Forgetting that isolation reduces the natural room sound many amp tones rely on
UNSAFE: Sealing an amp inside an unventilated enclosure for long periods, which lets it overheat and risks equipment damage or fire; keep manufacturer-specified ventilation clear.
scenario_contexts: Using an isolation cabinet so a loud amp can be miked in a home studio at night
Placing the guitar cab in a separate room to stop it bleeding into the drum mics
Recording a full-volume tube amp tone in a small studio without disturbing neighbors

sources: Guitar amplifier manufacturer safety documentation (ventilation and overheating warnings)
